title: Head Shaking / Ear Scratching
shortDescription: Occasional head shaking with a bright, eating dog is often ear irritation. A head tilt, bleeding, or a dog who cannot settle needs a same-day exam.
homeTriageChecklist: Confirm they are eating, drinking, and walking normally.
Look at the ear flap for redness, swelling, or a bad smell. Do not push anything into the canal.
Check gum color. Pink and moist is reassuring. Pale, blue, or brick-red gums are an emergency.
Count resting breaths for 15 seconds and multiply by four. A calm dog is often near 15–30 breaths per minute.
seekImmediateCareIf: The head is tilted and stays that way, or the dog walks in circles.
There is blood, a swollen ear flap, or crying when the mouth opens.
They are lethargic, vomiting, or have pale gums.
Shaking started after a fight, a fall, or a possible foreign body.
commonCauses: Ear mites, yeast, or bacterial irritation
Allergy flare or water left in the ear after swimming
A grass seed or other foreign body
Less often, a middle-ear or neurologic problem

title: Vomiting Yellow Bile
shortDescription: Yellow bile often means an empty stomach or gut irritation. One episode in a bright adult dog can be watched for a few hours if the belly is soft and the gums are pink. Repeated vomiting, blood, a puppy, or a tight abdomen needs a clinic the same day.
homeTriageChecklist: Check gum color and whether pink color returns in under 2 seconds.
Count resting breaths for 30 seconds and double the number. More than about 40 per minute at rest is an emergency.
Lift the skin over the shoulders and see if it flattens within about 2 seconds.
Touch the belly lightly. A tight, drum-like abdomen or unproductive retching is an emergency, not a bile problem to watch.
seekImmediateCareIf: They retch repeatedly and bring little up, or the belly looks swollen.
Vomit contains blood, coffee-ground material, or a possible toxin wrapper.
The dog is collapsed, has white or blue gums, or is having a seizure.
Vomiting continues more than two or three times, or they cannot keep water down.
commonCauses: Bilious vomiting from a long gap between meals, or dietary indiscretion
Intestinal parasites or a bacterial gut infection
Pancreatitis, kidney disease, or liver disease
A foreign-body blockage or a toxin such as chocolate, grapes, or xylitol
Bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus) or another collapse illness such as Addison's disease

title: Lethargy
shortDescription: A dog who is quieter than usual but still drinking and walking can be assessed the same day. Collapse, pale gums, or a dog who will not rise is an emergency.
homeTriageChecklist: Compare today's energy with their normal walk and greeting.
Check gum color and capillary refill by pressing a pink gum. Color should return in about 1–2 seconds.
Count resting breaths and note coughing or belly effort.
Record appetite, water intake, urine, and any new medicine or toxin access.
seekImmediateCareIf: They collapse, cannot stand, or seem confused.
Gums are pale, blue, yellow, or brick red.
The belly is swelling, they are straining to urinate, or they had a seizure.
A short-nosed dog is open-mouth breathing after heat or exercise.
commonCauses: Pain, fever, or an infection
Dehydration or an upset stomach
Anemia, heart disease, or internal bleeding
Toxin exposure or heatstroke

title: Limping or Not Using a Leg
shortDescription: A mild limp that eases after rest can be checked within 12–24 hours if the dog is otherwise well. A dangling limb, bleeding, or a dog hit by a car needs an emergency hospital.
homeTriageChecklist: Watch whether they put any weight on the leg.
Look for wounds, swelling, or a limb that hangs at an odd angle. Do not pull on it.
Check gum color and breathing so you do not miss shock after trauma.
Note stairs, jumps, or a fight in the last day.
seekImmediateCareIf: The leg dangles, has an open wound, or they will not put the foot down after trauma.
There is uncontrolled bleeding or they were hit by a car.
They are weak, have pale gums, or more than one leg is involved.
The limp appeared with a swollen belly, trouble breathing, or collapse.
commonCauses: Sprain, muscle strain, or a broken nail
A torn ligament or joint disease
A fracture or dislocation after a fall or car impact
A bite wound or foreign body in the paw

title: Collapse or Seizure
shortDescription: A dog who falls over, paddles, or cannot be woken needs an emergency clinic now. Keep hands away from the mouth during a seizure and time how long it lasts.
homeTriageChecklist: Move furniture away and dim noise. Do not restrain the body.
Time the episode and film it if you can do that safely.
When they are awake, check gum color and breathing rate.
Look for toxin packaging, heat exposure, or a bloated belly.
seekImmediateCareIf: This list is the emergency. Leave for a clinic after the first seizure or collapse.
A seizure lasts more than a couple of minutes or they have more than one.
They stay unconscious, have pale or blue gums, or cannot walk afterward.
The episode follows chocolate, xylitol, a fight, or heat.
commonCauses: Epilepsy or a first-time seizure disorder
Low blood sugar, toxin, or heatstroke
Heart rhythm problems or internal bleeding
Brain disease or severe pain

title: Straining in Litter Box
shortDescription: A cat who squats often and passes little or no urine may have a urethral blockage, especially if male. That is an emergency, not constipation, until a veterinarian proves otherwise.
homeTriageChecklist: Check the box for urine, not only stool. No urine is the danger sign.
Note crying, licking under the tail, or vomiting.
Look at gum color and whether the belly feels tight. Do not press hard.
Count resting breaths. Open-mouth breathing in a cat is an emergency on its own.
seekImmediateCareIf: A male cat strains and produces no urine, or only drops.
They vomit, hide, cry, or have a firm belly.
Gums are pale or they are too weak to walk.
You are unsure whether the problem is urine or stool. Go in.
commonCauses: Urethral obstruction from crystals, mucus, or spasm
Bladder inflammation that is painful but still letting urine pass
Constipation, which must be distinguished by a veterinarian
Urinary infection, less common in young male cats than inflammation

title: Drinking More Water
shortDescription: A cat who suddenly empties the water bowl needs a veterinary visit within a day, with a urine check. Collapse, vomiting, or straining to urinate should not wait for that appointment.
homeTriageChecklist: Note how often you refill the bowl compared with last week.
Watch appetite, weight, vomiting, and litter-box clumps.
Check gum moisture and whether they are still grooming.
Confirm they are passing urine. A blocked male cat can look restless around water and still be an emergency.
seekImmediateCareIf: They strain in the box, vomit repeatedly, or collapse.
They are a diabetic patient who is weak, or you smell a strong acetone odor.
Gums are pale or they are open-mouth breathing.
Thirst follows lily exposure, antifreeze, or another toxin.
commonCauses: Kidney disease or hyperthyroidism
Diabetes mellitus
A diet change or hot weather, if the increase is small and the cat is well
Urinary disease

title: Occasional Sneezing
shortDescription: A few sneezes in a cat who is eating and breathing quietly can be watched. Colored discharge, mouth ulcers, or any increase in breathing effort needs a clinic.
homeTriageChecklist: Confirm they are eating, drinking, and using the box.
Look for discharge from the eyes or nose. Clear and mild is less urgent than yellow or bloody.
Watch the chest from the side. Extra belly effort or open-mouth breathing is an emergency.
Check gum color if they allow a gentle look.
seekImmediateCareIf: They breathe with the mouth open, aside from a brief pant when stressed.
They stop eating, have facial swelling, or a nosebleed.
A kitten is sneezing and becoming quiet or dehydrated.
Sneezing started after a lily, cleaning product, or smoke exposure.
commonCauses: A mild viral upper-respiratory irritation
Dust, litter dust, or a scent in the home
Dental disease with nasal involvement
A foreign body or a more serious respiratory infection

title: Hiding and Not Eating
shortDescription: A cat who skips more than a meal or hides when they are usually social should see a veterinarian within 12–24 hours. Overweight cats can develop hepatic lipidosis if anorexia continues.
homeTriageChecklist: Note the last full meal and whether water intake changed.
Check the litter box for urine and stool.
Look at gum color and breathing effort without dragging them out roughly.
Scan for lilies, string, or a medicine bottle they could have reached.
seekImmediateCareIf: They strain to urinate, vomit repeatedly, or have a painful belly.
Gums are pale or yellow, or they collapse.
An overweight cat has not eaten for much of a day.
You saw string, a lily, or a toxin.
commonCauses: Pain, nausea, or fever
Dental disease or a foreign body
Urinary obstruction
Early liver or kidney illness

title: Tail Bobbing (Birds)
shortDescription: A rhythmic tail bob with each breath means the bird is working too hard to breathe. That is an avian emergency, even if they still look alert.
homeTriageChecklist: Watch from a short distance. Count whether the tail moves with every breath.
Note open-mouth breathing, a voice change, or sitting on the cage floor.
Check recent fumes: non-stick pans, aerosols, smoke, or strong cleaners.
Do not catch them repeatedly to inspect the chest. Stress can worsen hypoxia.
seekImmediateCareIf: The tail bobs at rest, or the beak stays open to breathe.
They are on the cage floor, fluffed, or too weak to perch.
There was fume exposure, an injury, or possible egg binding.
You are unsure. Birds compensate until they suddenly cannot.
commonCauses: Airway or lung disease, including infection
Fume exposure, such as overheated non-stick coatings
Egg binding or a mass pressing on the air sacs
Heart disease or anemia

title: Fluffed and Quiet
shortDescription: A bird who stays fluffed, quiet, and less interested in food is often ill even without dramatic signs. Arrange an avian visit the same day, and go now if breathing changes.
homeTriageChecklist: Compare droppings today with their normal color and volume.
Watch breathing for a tail bob or open beak.
Note the last time they ate millet, pellets, or their usual meal.
Weigh them if you already have a gram scale and can do it with almost no chase.
seekImmediateCareIf: They tail-bob, breathe with an open beak, or fall off the perch.
Droppings are absent, bloody, or mostly water in a weak bird.
They were exposed to fumes, a ceiling fan injury, or a cat bite.
A female is straining or standing wide-legged.
commonCauses: Infection or pain that the bird is hiding
A diet that is mostly seed, with vitamin deficiency over time
Reproductive disease or egg binding
Toxin or heavy-metal exposure

title: Routine Feather Molt
shortDescription: A gradual loss of worn feathers, with pin feathers and a normal appetite, is usually a molt. Bald patches, bleeding, or a fluffed bird on the floor are not a routine molt.
homeTriageChecklist: Confirm they are eating, playing, and perching as usual.
Look for symmetrical feather loss rather than one plucked bald spot.
Check droppings and breathing. A tail bob is unrelated to a normal molt.
Keep baths and humidity available if they already enjoy them. Do not oil the skin.
seekImmediateCareIf: Feathers are broken and bleeding, or the bird is self-mutilating.
They are fluffed, losing weight, or not eating.
Breathing is labored or they sit on the cage floor.
A cat or dog had contact with the bird.
commonCauses: A normal seasonal molt
Feather-destructive behavior or skin irritation
Infection or liver disease when molt is paired with illness
Injury from a cage mate or household pet

title: Teeth Grinding / Hunching (Rabbits)
shortDescription: Loud teeth grinding with a hunched posture is a pain signal in rabbits, often from the gut or teeth. It needs a rabbit-savvy veterinarian now, not a wait until tomorrow.
homeTriageChecklist: Look for fecal pellets. None, or very small pellets, raises concern for gut stasis.
Offer hay and see whether they take a bite. Do not force-feed an animal who cannot swallow.
Note drooling, a wet chin, or a preference for soft food, which can mean dental pain.
Check gum color if you can lift a lip gently. Pale gums or collapse means go immediately.
seekImmediateCareIf: They grind their teeth, hunch, and refuse hay.
Droppings have stopped or the belly feels gas-filled.
They are cold, limp, or breathing with effort.
There is diarrhea, especially in a young rabbit.
commonCauses: Gastrointestinal stasis and gas pain
Dental spurs or a tooth root abscess
A urinary stone or bladder sludge
A true obstruction, which is a surgical emergency

title: Fewer or Smaller Droppings
shortDescription: Smaller or fewer fecal pellets mean the gut is slowing. If the rabbit is still eating, call a rabbit veterinarian the same day. No pellets plus pain is an emergency.
homeTriageChecklist: Count pellets in the litter area compared with a normal day.
Watch hay intake. Hay matters more than pellets or treats.
Check posture for hunching and listen for loud tooth grinding.
Note urine and any soft uneaten cecotropes stuck to the fur.
seekImmediateCareIf: They stop eating entirely or have passed no pellets for about 12 hours.
They grind their teeth, press the belly to the floor, or feel bloated.
There is watery diarrhea, collapse, or a low body temperature.
A young rabbit is quiet and soiling the hind end.
commonCauses: Early gastrointestinal stasis
A low-fiber diet or not enough hay
Pain from teeth, urine, or an injury
A blockage from carpet, hair, or the wrong food

title: Mild Seasonal Shedding
shortDescription: A light, even shed in a rabbit or guinea pig who is eating hay and passing normal droppings can be groomed at home. Bald skin, scratching until it bleeds, or a hunched pet needs a clinic.
homeTriageChecklist: Confirm hay intake and a normal volume of droppings.
Brush loose undercoat gently. Stop if the skin is red or the pet struggles to breathe.
Part the coat and look for bald patches, dandruff, or moving specks.
Watch posture and appetite so shedding is not the only change you notice.
seekImmediateCareIf: They stop eating, grind their teeth, or pass fewer droppings.
Skin is raw, bleeding, or covered in crusts.
A guinea pig has a limp, labored breathing, or a swollen foot.
Hair is coming out in clumps after a new medicine or toxin.
commonCauses: A normal seasonal coat blow
Barbering by a cage mate
Mites or a skin infection
Pain or gut disease that happens to coincide with shedding
